items.content:
OpenWorker -- an open source agent that doesn't just chat but completes tasks on your laptop -- just released a new version with many features for security workflows. 

After our initial release, many users found it especially useful for cybersecurity. Attackers are already using AI; OpenWorker is committed to giving defenders the same leverage. Running an agent requires both (i) A model and (ii) A harness (the software around the model). Because the OpenWorker harness is fully open source, security teams can audit it to make sure we haven't built any backdoors that exfiltrate your code and data to some company or even a foreign adversary.

OpenWorker now comes with built-in cybersecurity agents for (i) Scanning your code for vulnerabilities. (ii) Scanning dependencies for supply chain injections. (iii) Checking your cloud security configuration for attack surfaces. This enables developers to do much more security work before deployment (part of what's called the "shift left" movement).

You choose the model: you can run open weight models fully locally so sensitive code never leaves your machine. This helps with legitimate security work (like reproducing a known exploit to defend against it) that can trigger refusals in leading closed models. Or use your ChatGPT subscription, or stealth preview models like Ox Alpha, or any model via API key.

Thanks also to all the open source contributors!

Join work with @rohitcprasad so please follow him too to get more frequent updates.

Putting this tweet in the “scary” category of AI.

Calling upon the non-technical business professionals that follow me
items.content:
Putting this tweet in the “scary” category of AI.

Calling upon the non-technical business professionals that follow me to pay attention. 

I’m breaking down the key parts of the @RyanGreenblatt tweet on the METR research covering the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident.

As background: METR is an independent 3P research non-profit that focuses on AI evaluations and risk assessments. They went to the OpenAI offices for 6 days to run these retros. METR takes no funding from AI companies and was not paid to do this research, but they used ~$400,000 in provided OpenAI credits to complete the research. Ryan is Chief Scientist at Redwood Research, who worked with METR on this, and he was in charge of the transcripts. 

This is a sign of what’s to come. 

1) Scale of understanding massive complex systems requires AI because a human can’t read 1300 transcripts, many with millions of tokens, in a few days - big bottlenecks of time and volume 

2) Humans become more reliant on AI for analysis and explanations of complex AI activity 

3) That process will get harder: 

a) AI may stop communicating in natural language either because it’s less efficient than shorthand code (which they used) or activations (numbers) or because AI agents will want to purposefully hide their reasoning from humans…making it harder to understand. 

b) The incidents may (and almost certainly will) get more complex…making it harder to understand. 

c) AI seems likely to get “smarter” and more capable (ex: better at tool handling, fewer errors, more complex orchestration, more clever at staying stealth or going undetected for longer) and may execute more sophisticated hacks…making it harder to understand. 

d) The AI running the investigation already had issues (incomplete, overconfident) and may be even less helpful in the future and could do more on hiding key details, incomplete answers, lying, or not answering…making it harder to understand. 

Reducing urgency and improving testing and prevention may help. Open reports like this one are also helpful to democratize the details (although, we are also democratizing the details for agents to scan). Seems likely we’ll see more open research in this area.

OpenAI is proposing to remove access to its models in Cursor on November 12. 

OpenAI, Cursor CEO, and Anthropic founder
items.content:
OpenAI is proposing to remove access to its models in Cursor on November 12. 

OpenAI, Cursor CEO, and Anthropic founder all weighed in on X with so much subtly, I had to go Nancy Drew mode and dissect each tweet. 

My translation of each one 👇 

OpenAI - they trust the Cursor team, they don’t trust SpaceX, it’s a “proposal” so maybe this public tweet is a way to gain leverage in the negotiation (note that it came from the company account on a Friday night)

Cursor - seems surprised about the OpenAI tweet, sounds like they want to fight it, goes out of their way to say OpenAI is a small percent of traffic, calls into question their neutrality (though I don’t think the labs call themselves neutral) (and note it came from the CEO, not the company account)

Anthropic - reaffirms the trust in Cursor and reminds us that it’s been years of trust, highlights they’re providing more of the most constrained carrot (compute), takes positive spin on the acquisition by SpaceX (note that it came from founder Tom who we don’t hear from often and not Anthropic account, and note that Cursor CEO reshared) 

Do I think it’ll hold? It’s hard for me to see a world where OpenAI continues to provide model access to a Musk-led company. Maybe if the structure of SpaceX shifts to allow for it, but that’s a big shift. 

Do I think Anthropic got a big PR boost? No, devs are focused on the loss of O, not the maintenance of partnership with A. They care about their own work. 

What’s the theme here? TRUST. How long has the trust been there, who holds the relationship, what hurt it, how to keep it. At the end of the day, all of these companies are led by people.

In 2023, a study from academic researchers in Switzerland found t
items.content:
Amazon is shutting down Mechanical Turk in September.

In 2023, a study from academic researchers in Switzerland found that up to 46% of AMT workers were using AI to complete their tasks. 

I can’t imagine that number got any lower, and I wouldn’t be surprised if 2026 numbers were 80%+ if the same study were to run again. 

I remember using AMT for data labeling a decade ago. We would have several labelers label/count each thing, and then look at consensus, variability, and risk of each thing before providing final labels. 

Unless these data labeling companies control the entire environment (ex: Scale AI opens an office that has human labelers come in every day), it’s a ripe opportunity for cheating. Just like asking kids to do their homework without any help from ChatGPT. 

We should assume that, even if they are asked not to do so or even if they sign a contract that they says they shouldn’t, humans outside of controlled environments will use AI to get something done if it gives them an advantage. 

For those of us who have been in AI 10+ years, this feels like a big deal. 

I feel nostalgic for easier AI times sometimes, and then I open up my Monday triage emails and Slacks from Claude Code and Codex and jump right back in.

items.content:
I was copying and pasting the same boilerplate around and it just didn't feel right.

So I built an open source library and put it out there.

Months later someone pulled me aside at an event in San Francisco and said they were using it. I asked who they were.

They said Oracle.

I had no company then. No pricing. No contract, no sales team. Twenty years of engineering and a library I had given away.

What I had not understood is that the people with the hardest problems find you first. Not hobbyists. Large enterprises, already in production, before you know they are there.

That is when I knew there was a business in it.

Not a market size. One person at an event telling me the decision had already been made without me.

So what was the signal?

Somebody with real money and real risk had committed before I had.

A lot of founders wait for a permission that never arrives. Go find out who is actually using your thing.

items.content:
There's a fascinating new startup using dogs to detect cancer in human breath

In a new trial, the dogs detected it over 90% of the time!

How it works:

Dognosis has patients breathe into a cotton surgical mask, which is then frozen and shipped to their farm in India.

There, a dog works a line of 10 samples. One beagle breezed past the first five, stopped at the sixth, moved away, came back, and circled it for several seconds.

To her, the whole thing is a game, and the reward is a treat.

But the dog is only half the system. Sensors track each dog's movement, body language, and brain activity.

A probabilistic model then combines signals from multiple dogs, weighted by each dog's historical accuracy, into a single score.

In a study of over 3,000 people, that system caught 90.8% of the real cancers, and correctly cleared 91.3% of the people who didn't have any.

The catch is that this was from a case-control study, where researchers already knew who had cancer (finding rare cases hidden in a healthy population is a harder problem).

BUT a larger trial is running now across 10 Indian hospitals.

If it holds up, we might use dogs to help detect cancer in the future

items.title: Launch HN: Almanac (YC S26) – AI that knows your company
items.content:
Launch HN: Almanac (YC S26) – AI that knows your company Hi HN, I'm Kushagra, one of three founders of Almanac, a Hermes with a brain that knows everything about your company.

We started our journey with setting up Hermes for our company, thinking it must be easy. We wanted an agent that would know every context about our company, so we could ask questions and get context-appropriate responses to.

This started a very annoying and difficult journey. Setting up Hermes, getting it to talk right, building OAuth apps for every connector myself, then feeding it context myself, and ultimately struggling with Hermes's default memory. At the same time, we saw our YC batchmates struggling with the same problem, and we saw an opportunity.

So we built Almanac. This is how it works. You sign up, you get a Hermes agent straight out of the box. You have a one-click connect to any account (Gmail, Calendar, Granola, PostHog, etc). You have personal accounts (only accessible by you) and also shared accounts (accessible by everyone in the company). The consequence being I can never see my cofounders' accounts.

The “brain” of this agent is wikis. We pull in information from your connected sources, and start organizing this information in two wikis. A personal one, for you, which understands who you are, what your preferences are, the people in your life, and the things going on in your life. The second wiki is a company wiki, which includes what the company is, what you’re working on, what the roadmap is, and what the blockers of the company are. Your agent ultimately has access to these two wikis and the original accounts, which invoke the feeling of “it just knows you.”

Here’s a demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ajXP5PHuK18

We're three cofounders, Rohan, Kushagra, and Divit, and we've been friends for 11 years, since studying for the IIT-JEE. We all did Electrical Engineering (Rohan at IIT Delhi, me at IIT Kharagpur, Divit at BITS Pilani, Hyderabad), and Rohan and I later went to Harvard, where this pre-compilation layer became our capstone thesis. We have built multiple products around the idea of a pre-compiled knowledge layer.

Our main differentiating point is the way we approach memory and context in general. Most AI assistant tools treat memory as an afterthought. We have worked on wikis for AI for more than a year now, building products for Harvard and NASA. The one thing we have learnt is that one needs to spend a lot more compute upfront, in the pre-compilation of this knowledge base, to get it right.

Having this pre-compiled knowledge base enables a lot of interesting ideas. First is a proactive agent. Since I have compiled what’s going on in both my company and my current life, Almanac can start completing tasks on its own. Concretely, we run a background worker which takes a look at tasks that could be completed, pings the main agent, who then pings me, suggesting which tasks it could automate. As a result, I wake up to proactive notifications which look like “I already prepared a draft of your fundraising pitch deck, want to take a look?”

Second, long-horizon tasks. In our wikis, we maintain a section on ongoing projects, so Almanac can pick a task back up days later without losing the thread. Most agents are session-bound: they run once, finish, and forget. But a lot of real work isn't one shot; it plays out over hours and days with people in the loop. The clearest example is anything that involves waiting on a human, like scheduling a meeting, following up on a sales thread, or chasing a document. Almanac can send an email on your behalf, and because it's always on and remembers the project, it notices the reply four hours later and drafts the right follow-up in context.

Since launching, we've seen a lot of use cases for Almanac. One person runs her dog-rescue operation through it: finding available fosters, tracking pickups, and sending reminders for consent forms. Another researches Polymarket strategies with Almanac, where its memory holds what past strategies were, proposes new ones, and compares them against what went right or wrong last time. Another builds marketing campaigns on it without having to re-explain the business and the whole campaign every single time.

Regarding privacy and security, Almanac only accesses accounts you explicitly connect. Your OAuth credentials are held by our connection provider, not in Almanac’s database. We only store the wiki and the source behind its citations. So an email used as a citation may be retained as Markdown.

We’re live: https://usealmanac.com. We have a 7-day trial on all of our plans. Happy to hear if people have done similar setups, and what new features they’d like in Almanac. If you’re a company that wants to get an agent that actually gets tasks done, I would love to talk: https://cal.com/team/almanac/demo.

You pay $20/month for a Claude subscription. But you still hit the limit by 2 pm. I did too, until I understood how Claude calculates credits: 

It re-reads the entire chat every time you send a prompt. Prompt 30 costs about 31x more than message 1. 

Upload the same PDF to 5 chats & you pay for it 5 times. Run Opus on a grammar check & you pay Opus prices for a Haiku job.

Here are the stupid simple 9 fixes to use every day:

FIX 1. Shrink your files.

Open a Google Doc. Paste the text from your PDF.
Download it as a .md file and upload that instead.
A 15-page PDF costs ~45,000 tokens.
The same text as .md costs ~2,000.

FIX 2. Plan in Chat, then build in Cowork.

In Claude Chat, prompt: "Help me plan a [financial model]. Ask me questions first."
Paste the finished plan into Cowork & say: "Build exactly this."

FIX 3. Let Claude prompt you instead.

A 500-word prompt costs 500 tokens. 
A click costs almost zero.
So prompt: "I want to [TASK] to [SUCCESS CRITERIA]. Ask me questions using AskUserQuestion before you start."

Full guide here: https://t.co/KNO2y4RkYr

FIX 4. Edit your last message.

If you want to correct a mistake, go to your sent prompt, click "Edit" on your message, retype your prompt, and hit Save.
Claude regenerates from that point.

FIX 5. Summarize every 15 prompts chat.

Prompt: "Summarize this entire conversation into a brief." Copy the brief. Paste it as message # 1 in a new chat. Turning 105,000 tokens into 500.

FIX 6. Pick the model before you start.

Open the model dropdown in the chatbox.
Under 30 seconds of thinking? Sonnet.
Execution, multi-step work? Opus.
Brainstorming or solving a complex problem? Fable

FIX 7. Use Projects for repeated files.

Create a Project. Upload your files there once. Every chat inside that Project reads them without re-tokenizing.

FIX 8. Turn off the settings that a task doesn't need.

Go to the tools panel. Turn off Web Search, connectors unless this specific task needs them.
Every idle feature adds tokens.

FIX 9. Batch your asks.

Send "Summarize this, list the key points, and write a headline" as ONE message. Three separate messages make Claude reload the full context three times.

items.content:
A simple mental framework for how long an agent takes to complete a task:

A task can essentially be broken down into the number of tokens by the implementation model x its harness needed to achieve it.

Consider a very difficult task, a very smart model might need to iterate 10x before it gets it right, and might require 10mn toks.

A less smart model might need to iterate 1000x before it gets it right, and might require 1bn toks. 

A dumb model will never get it right even if you let it iterate 1mn times, and will require an infinite toks.

--
Between the very smart model and the less smart model above, if the very smart model outputs tokens at 10 tok/s and the less smart model outputs tokens at 1000 tok/s, they actually complete the task at the same time.

So it's not JUST about intelligence.

The same thing is true about costs, it's temping to look at $/mn toks and state that a model is cheaper than another, but what you're actually interested in is the $/difficult task for the work you are doing. 

The "more expensive" model might end up using $100 for $10/mn toks for 10mn toks to complete the task, while the "less expensive" model might end up using $1000 for $1/mn toks for 1bn toks to complete the task.

--
Lastly, there are some tasks where anything LESS than frontier (e.g. Fable) literally cannot iterate towards the correct solution.

This is why frontier models continue to be very attractive even if cheaper models are available. 

Until a supermajority of "very hard" tasks can be solved by OSS models, OpenAI and Anthropic will likely continue winning over more and more prosumers.

--
Bonus: There are some domains that are "so difficult", which is another way of saying that the solution space is so far away from the training data available to the models (e.g. quant finance), that you will literally need to provide iterative feedback for the model to arrive at a reasonable solution.

A developer in China recorded a 2 minute Claude Code tutorial, expecting only a few hundred people to watch it.

Then someone noticed something unusual at the 47 second mark.

The second monitor showed a Polymarket wallet with:

$868,862 in profits
28,620 Bitcoin trades in 15 minutes
No recorded losses
Entry prices between 2 and 10 cents
Payouts reaching thousands of dollars

The tutorial was deleted just 3 hours later.

But by then, the screenshot had already spread.

The clip reportedly reached 400,000 views, while more than 707,000 people were tracking the wallet.

items.content:
Just finished mapping out the entire AI tooling landscape.

The data is fascinating, but the real story is in the connections.

Here’s my unfiltered take: The "Agentic AI" category is a misnomer. That’s the brain (the LLMs). The real "Agent" is the nervous system coordinating all the other parts.

Let me walk you through the blueprint of a modern AI stack:

1. The Brain (Foundation Models)
We've got deep pockets here. It’s no longer just OpenAI vs. Anthropic. The rise of open-weight models (Llama, Mistral) and the infrastructure to run them (Ollama, vLLM) is democratizing the core intelligence. The choice here defines your system's "personality."

2. The Nervous System (Orchestration & RAG)
This is where the magic happens. LangGraph and CrewAI are dominating the multi-agent workflow space. But look at Microsoft AutoGen and AWS Strands, the cloud giants are building their own moats. They're not just connecting to a database; they are routing tasks between specialized agents.

 3. The Memory (Short & Long-term)
This is the hardest problem to solve. Tools like Memo and Zep are building "stateful" agents, while LangGraph Memory is trying to make it native to the graph. The secret sauce? It's not just about what you remember, but how you retrieve it. This is where Vector DBs (Pinecone, Qdrant) and Graph DBs (Neo4j) intersect.

4. The Eyes (Embedding & Retrieval)
RAGFlow and GraphRAG are pushing the boundaries beyond keyword search. They are moving towards semantic understanding and knowledge graphs. The choice of BGE vs. Voyage AI for embeddings is becoming a strategic decision based on domain specificity.

5. The Immune System (Security & Guardrails)
Production is scary. NVIDIA NeMo and Guardrails AI are the bouncers at the club, ensuring outputs stay on-brand and safe. If you don't have a "Guardrails" layer, you don't have a production system.

6. The Vital Signs (Observability)
You can't fix what you can't see. LangSmith and Langfuse are the dashboards for the AI brain. They’re moving beyond logging to tracing the chain of thought. Ragas and TruLens are specifically for evaluating the retrieval quality—a crucial win condition.

 7. The Hands (Agent SDKs)
Finally, we have the execution layer. OpenAI Agents SDK vs. LangChain Agents vs. PydanticAI. The trend is clear: frameworks are getting lighter and more pythonic. The goal is to move from "building a robot" to "writing a script."

The Big Picture:
This isn't just a spreadsheet of tools. It’s a modular brain. The winners won't be the ones with the best single component, but the ones who can chain them together seamlessly.

We are moving from "Prompt Engineering" to "System Architecture."

AI SaaS products often fail for reasons other than the agent simply giving a bad answer

They might lose state mid-task or time out during a long generation process, while the founder discovers the model budget has been blown only when it’s too late

Three repositories address these issues at different layers:

▸ Agno ★42K

A platform for AI agents featuring APIs, session state management, memory, tools, logging, and manual approval steps

Ideal when the agent needs to handle more than just text—such as files, external services, and multi-step workflows

▸ Inngest ★5.8K

A long-running task shouldn't have to restart from scratch just because a single API call failed

Inngest breaks workflows into resilient steps; features like retries, scheduling, concurrency limits, and error recovery are built right into the scenario

Useful for report generation, file processing, and agent tasks that take minutes or hours to complete

▸ Helicone ★6.1K

An observability layer for LLMs

It tracks requests, latency, costs, and experiment results, ensuring the AI ​​component of your product doesn't remain a "black box."

A proven workflow:

request or file → Agno
→ long-running task and retries → Inngest
→ cost, errors, and quality → Helicone
→ human confirms critical action

Don't try to cram all of this into your first chatbot

Agno is overkill for a simple FAQ bot. Inngest is only necessary for long-running or unreliable processes. And you shouldn't blindly send personal data or secrets to Helicone logs

$QUBIC : Review 📜

What if every watt the mining industry burns solving meaningless puzzles could be pointed at building artificial intelligence instead, and the papers proving it worked were already published?

Meet Qubic, a Layer 1 built on Useful Proof of Work, where miners compete
to produce the best neural networks rather than the most hashes. It holds the highest verified mainnet throughput of any blockchain at 15.52 million TPS, its AI research now appears in peer-reviewed AGI proceedings, and its token is spendable at a claimed fifty million merchants.

Let's explore the most technically ambitious project in the series. 👇

⚪ Qubic at a Glance

Marketplace Insight: Qubic sits in the AI compute category alongside Render, Akash, and io net, but attacks the problem one layer deeper. Rather than renting GPUs, it makes AI production the byproduct of securing the chain. For a long time the fair criticism was that the AI end remained a research programme with nothing to show.

August 2026 changed that materially: a Multi-Neuraxon paper published in Springer's AGI-26 proceedings, a best oral presentation at IEEE AMLDS in Osaka, and an ARC-AGI-3 score around 0.25 achieved on CPUs with no LLM involved. The clean contrast now is not between promise and delivery but between scientific validation and commercial scale. The research is real and peer-reviewed. Whether it becomes a product anyone pays for is the open question.

⚪ Mission

Qubic exists to make consensus productive and to reach artificial general intelligence through distributed computation. The founding argument is that proof-of-work secures networks by wasting energy on deliberately useless work, and that the same security can come from work that produces something valuable. The chosen output is Aigarth, a system that evolves neural networks rather than training a static model. The deeper thesis is that AI's binding constraint is economic rather than algorithmic, and that a global mining network is the only structure capable of supplying compute at the necessary scale.

🔵 A Brief History

Qubic was founded by Sergey Ivancheglo, better known as Come-from-Beyond, one of crypto's more polarizing technical figures. He co-founded NXT, the first pure proof-of-stake blockchain, and later IOTA, arriving at Qubic with a record of genuine innovation and combative execution in roughly equal measure.

The architecture was unusual from the start: 676 elected Computors governing by quorum, bare-metal execution with no virtual machine, and weekly epochs emitting exactly 1 trillion QUBIC. In 2024, a community vote called Project X cut maximum supply from 1,000 trillion to 200 trillion and introduced the halving schedule and SupplyWatcher contract driving the token's deflation.

2025 produced both the technical high point and the reputational flashpoint. CertiK certified a mainnet throughput record of 15.52 million TPS, unmatched by any other chain. Then between May and August, Qubic's share of Monero's hashrate climbed from under 2% toward a claimed majority, with Ivancheglo openly announcing plans to demonstrate 51% control. A six-block reorganization was detected, Ledger's CTO stated publicly that Monero appeared to be under a successful 51% attack, and XMR fell sharply. The Monero community coordinated a boycott and answered with sustained DDOS attacks. Qubic described the episode as a combative application of game theory.

2026 has been about converting theory into shipped systems. The first halving raised the burn rate to 55%, Dogecoin ASIC mining launched in parallel with Monero and AI workloads, and August delivered the densest month yet: the BPP-9000 Useful Proof of Work algorithm went live rewarding the lowest-error neural networks rather than raw hash volume, Ant Colony Mining activated so miners build on each other's retained best solutions, Outsourced Computing reached mainnet letting contracts act on the outside world, QubicPay launched with AEON Pay across roughly fifty million merchants, the second halving executed on schedule, and the Aigarth research team published in Springer's AGI-26 proceedings.

🔵 Ecosystem Narrative

The organizing idea is that computation should produce value twice, once as security and once as intelligence.

➛ BPP-9000 and quality-based mining. The new Useful Proof of Work algorithm rewards the best solutions, specifically the lowest-error small neural networks predicting Bitcoin price direction, rather than raw hash volume, so miners compete on quality of output rather than energy expended.

➛ Ant Colony Mining. Activated in late August, miners now build on each other's retained top solutions, with the network keeping the 676 best results each cycle, so search compounds across the network instead of thousands of participants duplicating isolated work.

➛ Aigarth and Neuraxon. Peer-reviewed and published: a Multi-Neuraxon architecture of four specialized brain regions handling vision, hearing, association, and movement, self-organizing and communicating through frequency gating, remaining functional after large neuron loss, with an ARC-AGI-3 score near 0.25 on CPUs without an LLM.

➛ QubicPay and AEON Pay. The token is spendable at a claimed fifty million merchants across Asia, Latin America, and Africa through existing local rails including UPI, Pix, VietQR, and SPEI, with merchants receiving ordinary local-currency QR payments and consumers using a Telegram Mini App.

➛ Outsourced Computing. Live on mainnet, completing the third pillar so smart contracts can act on the outside world rather than remaining sealed within the chain.

➛ Developer infrastructure. The AIO Dev Kit gives free local build-and-test for smart contracts, replacing a previously costly IPO-style testing model, alongside a dedicated developer channel and a trustless BFrost bridge in development using oracles and zero-knowledge proofs.

⚪ Token Utilities

$QUBIC functions as computational energy rather than a conventional gas token.

➛ Computation: burned when executing smart contracts and consuming network services, so usage directly destroys supply.

➛ Computor rewards: the 676 elected Computors earn from weekly emissions, with distribution weighted by operational efficiency.

➛ Smart contract IPOs: new contracts launch through Dutch auctions that burn the proceeds, adding a second structural burn.

➛ Payments: spendable through QubicPay and AEON Pay at merchant networks across three continents, with fiat on-ramps through Alchemy Pay covering 173 countries.

⚪ Key Features

➛ Useful Proof of Work rewarding the best neural networks rather than the most hashes.

➛ Ant Colony Mining, where the network's search compounds rather than duplicates.

➛ A CertiK-certified mainnet record of 15.52 million TPS with feeless transactions.

➛ Peer-reviewed Aigarth research published in Springer AGI-26 proceedings.

➛ Merchant payments across roughly fifty million endpoints via local rails.

➛ An escalating burn schedule reaching 77.5% of weekly emissions.

🔵 Meet the Team

Qubic pairs a founder with genuine protocol-building history against a scientific advisory bench that publishes in academic venues, which is unusual for a project of this size and is the clearest signal that the AI work is real research rather than positioning.

▶️ Core Members:

➛ Sergey Ivancheglo, CFB [ @c___f___b ]  - Founder | Co-founded NXT, the first pure proof-of-stake blockchain, and later IOTA, giving him a rare record of foundational protocol innovation. He designed the Useful Proof of Work model and the Aigarth thesis, and remains the network's principal technical voice.

➛ David Vivancos [ @VivancosDavid ]  - Scientific Advisor | Brings external scientific credibility to the Aigarth research programme, part of the advisory bench behind the Neuraxon architecture and the work presented at IEEE AMLDS 2026 and published in Springer's AGI-26 proceedings.

➛ Dr. Jose Sánchez - Scientific Advisor | An academic advisor on the AI research side, supporting the peer-reviewed work on three-state Neuraxon neurons, self-organized criticality, and the multi-region architecture that reached publication this year.

➛ Stephanie Nickolich - Head of Marketing and Growth | Leads marketing and growth across the ecosystem, carrying a genuinely technical story, useful mining and decentralized AGI, out to an audience that mostly evaluates crypto on simpler terms.

➛ JoeTom - Developer and Advisor, and Raika - Developer | Core contributors on the engineering side, working across the protocol and the systems shipped through 2026 including BPP-9000, Ant Colony Mining, Outsourced Computing, and the AIO Dev Kit.

➛ The Computors | The load-bearing governance entity. 676 elected node operators who run the network, execute computation, and vote by quorum on protocol decisions including the supply cap reduction from 1,000 trillion to 200 trillion and both halvings. Governance here is operational rather than advisory.

🔵 Ratings

➛ Use Case: ★★★★★ (5/5). Qubic occupies a category it effectively created and delivers on it with independently verified results. Useful Proof of Work is a fundamental answer to AI's economic constraint rather than a marketplace layered on top of it, the 15.52 million TPS mainnet record is CertiK-certified and unmatched by any blockchain, and BPP-9000 with Ant Colony Mining turns global mining into a compounding quality search rather than brute force. Critically, the AI output is now externally validated: peer-reviewed publication in Springer's AGI-26 proceedings, a best oral presentation at IEEE AMLDS, and a measurable ARC-AGI-3 score achieved on ordinary CPUs without a language model. Add Outsourced Computing on mainnet, QubicPay reaching roughly fifty million merchants, and parallel Dogecoin and Monero mining running alongside AI training, and this is a project doing things nobody else in crypto is attempting, with the receipts to prove it works.

➛ Tokenomics: ★★★★ (4/5). This is one of the more aggressive and better-executed deflationary designs in crypto, and it executes on schedule. The community voted to cut maximum supply from 1,000 trillion to 200 trillion, weekly emissions stay fixed while the burned share escalates through halvings from 15% to 55% and now 77.5% as of August 19, 41.5 trillion tokens have already been destroyed, the SupplyWatcher adjusts dynamically, and smart contract IPOs burn their proceeds. Usage directly destroys supply. The 1-point deduction is that net emissions remain positive at roughly 225 billion weekly even after the second halving, so the token is decelerating rather than deflating, and Computors have raised genuine concerns about a shrinking reward pool as the burn rate climbs.

➛ Audits: ★★★★ (4/5). Qubic's security posture is stronger than most projects at this market cap and is backed by CertiK's direct involvement, which certified the network's 15.52 million TPS record on mainnet, a level of independent technical verification few chains submit to at all. The bare-metal architecture structurally removes an entire class of virtual machine vulnerabilities that affect most smart contract platforms, and the network has operated for years without a protocol-level exploit while withstanding a sustained DDOS campaign. The project is also running a transparent public security post-mortem, with 7 of 9 remediation items complete and the remainder targeted for end of September. The 1-point deduction is that no verified top-tier security score or named formal verification is published, and the newest systems including BPP-9000, Ant Colony Mining, and Outsourced Computing add substantial fresh surface still accruing operating history.

➛ Community: ★★★★★ (5/5). Qubic has one of the most active and genuinely committed communities in crypto, and the engagement is measurable rather than claimed. Its X presence is consistently among the loudest in the AI-crypto category, the community absorbed a sustained DDOS campaign and coordinated hostility from a rival network without fragmenting, and governance functions operationally through 676 elected Computors who have approved consequential economic decisions including the supply cap reduction and both halvings. Developer momentum is now visible too, with the AIO Dev Kit removing a real cost barrier, a dedicated developer channel, open science AMAs, and researchers presenting at IEEE and AGI conferences. Few projects at this market cap sustain this level of participation across governance, mining, development, and research at once. The community's intensity is also its edge: it is combative in a way that has made Qubic enemies as readily as advocates.

🔵 Conclusion

Qubic is the most technically audacious project in this series, and August 2026 was the month it closed the gap between ambition and evidence. The Useful Proof of Work model now rewards the quality of neural networks rather than raw hashing, Ant Colony Mining makes the network's search compound rather than duplicate, Outsourced Computing lets contracts reach the outside world, the token is spendable across three continents, and the second halving executed exactly as scheduled. Most importantly, Aigarth stopped being a claim: peer-reviewed publication, a conference award, and a measurable benchmark score achieved on ordinary CPUs without a language model.

The risks are worth naming honestly. Net emissions remain positive despite the aggressive burn schedule, and the halving passed without market reaction, suggesting the mechanism is better understood by the protocol than by the market. The newest systems are days old rather than battle-tested. And the Monero episode remains part of the project's public record, an act of combative game theory that cost it standing with parts of the industry regardless of what the science now produces.

But the bull case is genuinely distinctive. If AI compute economics are the binding constraint of the coming decade, a network that produces intelligence as a byproduct of securing itself is working a level below every GPU marketplace, and it now has peer-reviewed results rather than assertions. Qubic has proven it can build things nobody else has built, verify them independently, and get the output published in academic proceedings. What it still has to prove is that the world will pay for what it makes.

ok here's why each one actually matters - i ran all three

i tested it on my own obsidian vault + claude code stack.
turns out the fancy option is rarely the one you open daily.

1 / obsidian graph vs flat folder + search            
ngl the graph is the prettiest thing i never use.
when i need a note i hit cmd+o and type three letters.
the graph tells me i have a lot of notes.
search gives me the one i wanted.
flat folders + fast search beat topology you never traverse.

2 / skills marketplace vs skills you wrote

marketplace skills work fine. they just don't know my workflow.
mine knows my email setup, my folder names, the gotchas
i already debugged into the file.
a generic skill is someone else's defaults. yours is yours.
CLAUDE.md + a custom skill = context you paid for in failures.

3 / multi-agent swarm vs codex + claude consulting

i have an architecture diagram too. mine's just simpler.
the value didn't come from how many agents are on it.
it came from claude consulting my codex builder.
and codex consulting claude back.
they write proposals to each other, catch blind spots.
what reaches me is sharper than either would've shipped alone.

the uncomfortable part

everyone ships swarm diagrams.
the win is two models arguing before you see the diff.
one bot reviews. one bot builds. you approve.

3 moves if you're setting this up tonight:
1. kill the graph guilt - wire cmd+o search as your real vault ui
2. fork one marketplace skill, paste your folder names + gotchas in
3. make codex and claude exchange a proposal before any merge

limits: graph traversal still wins for evolving knowledge bases.
marketplace skills ship faster on day one.
cross-consult burns tokens - use it on architecture, not typos.
